source.title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression
source.authors: Mingyue Xu; Gal Vardi; Itay Safran

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent cut-off or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed generalization and its dependence on training hyperparameters using regression losses in ridge regression and neural networks, rather than the original algorithmic-task accuracy setup.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theorems and experiments report training and generalization behavior and hyperparameter effects. Related-work results are not recorded as rows. Figure-only experiments are included only where the text explicitly describes their outcome.
record.test_reason: The study proves and simulates delayed generalization (train loss below ε long before test loss below c) in over-parameterized ridge regression, random-feature and two-layer ReLU regression. It varies weight decay, initialization scale, sample size and width. This is a new, non-algorithmic setting with its own results on the training-regime and weight-decay versions (V3, V5). Its exact-arithmetic, plain-GD proof also bears on the artifact account (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove end-to-end grokking in over-parameterized ridge regression: fast training fit, long-persisting poor generalization, then eventual generalization. They give quantitative bounds showing the delay can be amplified or eliminated by hyperparameters, chiefly weight decay (t2 ∝ 1/λ) and initialization scale. The mechanism is slow weight-decay shrinkage of the null-space weight component. They conclude grokking is a consequence of specific training conditions rather than an inherent failure mode of deep learning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses randomly initialized gradient descent with ℓ2 weight decay on realizable ridge regression, random-feature networks, and ReLU networks, rather than the original modular-arithmetic algorithmic dataset setup. The main measurements are squared losses rather than accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported delay changes with weight decay, sample size, and initialization scale in some settings; increasing feature dimension has little effect in ridge regression. In random ReLU features, initialization scale does not significantly prolong grokking, and increased width does not significantly prolong it. Nonlinear-network and Fourier-feature results are reported as qualitative or requiring careful tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: In regression the continuous test loss decays smoothly with no plateau. A threshold-based surrogate accuracy recovers the familiar plateau, which the authors call an artifact of discrete metrics in classification.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The abrupt test-accuracy jump in grokking is partly a product of discrete accuracy metrics; continuous losses show smooth delayed improvement.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Experimental trend values are mostly reported through plots and qualitative descriptions rather than numerical tables. Some experiments are non-realizable or only described qualitatively, and the initialization-scale effect differs between ridge regression and random ReLU features.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 plots train/test losses over 50 independent runs for ridge regression and a fully trained two-layer ReLU network, but the text gives no explicit outcome values for those individual plots beyond identifying them as illustrations. The Figure 6 comparison across noise levels is noted in R13; no separate row was made because the text gives no exact levels or values.

untested.parts: Images, text or molecules are not tested; data are synthetic Gaussian/ReLU-teacher regression. A lazy-to-rich transition is not tested. The authors frame their mechanism as a ridgeless-to-ridge (misspecified-to-well-specified prior) transition and call proving lazy-to-rich an open question.
No competing circuits, efficiency comparison, critical dataset size or ungrokking are tested.
Adaptive optimizers and floating-point/softmax effects are not run as controls. The bearing on V7 comes only from the delay existing under exact-arithmetic plain GD.
No algorithmic datasets and no accuracy chance-to-perfect jump. The sample-size trend appears only in regression.

missing.what: Surrogate accuracy Px((N−N*)² ≤ ε) shows a plateau-then-jump while the squared loss decays smoothly. Run from one simulation with m=10000, n=100, λ=1e-5.
missing.locator: Section 6 final paragraph; Appendix B, Figure 5

missing.what: Different label-noise levels do not change grokking time by much.
Empirical t1 and t2 match the theoretical bounds of Eq. (8) across all four ridge sweeps (dashed vs solid lines).
Train/test loss curves over 50 independent runs for ridge regression and a fully trained two-layer ReLU network, both with a zero teacher.
missing.locator: Figure 1; setup at end of Section 5.3

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: a new regression setting with its own theory and simulations, not the original algorithmic method. The study proposes a ridgeless-to-ridge mechanism and explicitly leaves lazy-to-rich unproven, which matters for V3's parenthetical. The V7 challenge is indirect: the delay exists under plain GD in exact arithmetic, but no artifact controls were run. Most empirical values are plotted, not tabulated; rows R4–R14 rest on captions and text.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not use small algorithmic datasets or report training/test accuracy at chance and near-perfect levels, nor does it test the delay as training-set size shrinks in the claimed algorithmic setting.
It does not measure the formation of a generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or continuous mechanistic progress measures.

It studies synthetic regression, random-feature networks, and ReLU networks, not images, text, or molecules. It varies initialization scale and weight decay but does not analyze a lazy-to-rich transition or show that grokking can always be switched fully on or off.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.

It tests weight-decay effects on delay and discusses norm/complexity, but does not identify a more efficient generalizing circuit, establish a critical dataset size, or test ungrokking below such a size.
It does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits, or control these proposed artifacts.

relationships.condition: Ridge regression (theory and simulation), random ReLU features, fully trained two-layer ReLU network, label-noise ridge regression
relationships.reason: Theorems and simulations show early train fit followed by long-delayed generalization on non-algorithmic regression (R1, R2, R3, R12, R13). The delay is tuned by weight decay and, in ridge regression, by initialization scale: t1 and t2 scale as ln(ν²), so the gap widens (R4, R5, R7, R8, R9).
relationships.display_finding: Generalization followed early training fit after a long delay controlled by weight decay, with ridge-regression times t1 and t2 scaling as ln(ν²) and their gap widening.

relationships.condition: Random ReLU features and random Fourier features
relationships.reason: Raising initialization scale does not significantly prolong grokking in random ReLU features (R11). The Fourier-feature grokking appears only with careful hyperparameter tuning (R14).
relationships.display_finding: Increasing initialization scale did not significantly prolong grokking with random ReLU features, while random Fourier features exhibited grokking only after careful hyperparameter tuning.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Random ReLU features and random Fourier features
source_check.reason: R11 explicitly reports no significant prolongation from increasing initialization scale; R14 reports that observing grokking requires careful hyperparameter tuning. These qualify the generality of regime-based control.

relationships.condition: Weight-decay sweeps in ridge regression and random ReLU features
relationships.reason: Weight decay slowly shrinks the null-space component, driving the model toward the low-norm ridge solution that generalizes. t2 ∝ 1/λ, and the delay grows without bound as λ→0 (R2, R4, R8). Only the low-norm-bias part of V5 is tested.
relationships.display_finding: Weight decay slowly shrank the null-space component toward a generalizing low-norm ridge solution, with generalization time proportional to 1/λ and diverging as λ approached zero.

source_check.reason: R2, R4 and R8 support the low-norm-bias component: weight decay shrinks the null-space component, and smaller decay delays generalization. Circuit competition, a critical dataset size and ungrokking remain untested.

relationships.display_finding: The analysis proved a delay growing with 1/λ without adaptive optimization or softmax numerics, rather than testing their removal experimentally.
